text: Every instance you've provisioned earlier in this path shared a cost structure built around commodity CPU, memory, and storage. GPU instances break that pattern completely, and the gap is bigger than most new teams expect. Before you can optimize GPU cost, you need to understand exactly why it behaves so differently from every other cloud bill you've managed.

The premium starts with the hardware itself. A GPU card like an NVIDIA A100 or H100 is specialized silicon, produced at a tiny fraction of the volume of a CPU, built around expensive high-bandwidth memory and fast interconnects like NVLink. None of that shows up in a standard VM's price. And for years, demand for this hardware has outstripped supply, which keeps on-demand rates high across every cloud offering it.

To build intuition without pretending to know next quarter's exact pricing: a general-purpose CPU VM might run roughly one to two dollars an hour on demand, while a single high-end GPU instance from the same cloud can run ten to forty times that, and a multi-GPU instance scales close to linearly from there. Treat those as rough, illustrative ratios, not real published prices - the exact numbers shift by region, generation, and cloud.

That multiplier changes what a mistake costs. Leaving a standard VM running overnight by accident wastes a few dollars. Leaving a GPU instance running the same way wastes the same hours at ten to forty times the rate. Oversizing follows the same logic - provisioning a multi-GPU instance for a job that only needs one GPU means paying the full multi-GPU premium for capacity that never gets used. And a stuck or duplicated training job doesn't waste one GPU's worth of spend, it wastes however many GPUs the job spans, for every hour nobody notices.

That's the core problem this chapter solves: GPU spend moves faster than any other line item on your bill, so the FinOps habits from earlier in this path still apply, but the tolerance for catching a mistake late is much smaller. Next lesson looks at spot GPUs - a real discount worth taking seriously, alongside the real risk of losing an in-progress training run to interruption, and how checkpointing is what makes that tradeoff survivable.
